title: Can Fisher's Principle Limit Mother's Curse?
h1: Can the pull toward an even sex ratio stop mitochondria from harming males?
question: Can Fisher's principle put a limit on mitochondrial variants that harm males?
answer: A 2026 Frontiers in Genetics review by John Tower argues that it can. Mitochondria pass only through mothers, so variants that harm only males can spread. But when males become scarce, each male's reproductive fitness rises, and selection pushes back. The review's models suggest the two forces can balance, keeping moderately male-harming variants around.

event.name: Frontiers in Genetics publishes John Tower's review "Mother's curse meets Fisher's principle: uniparental mitochondrial inheritance and sex ratio in the genetics of aging"

artefact.text: The review is open access, with its three models, figures and the studies that do not fit.
artefact.label: Read the review

timeline.text: Frontiers in Genetics receives the review from John Tower of the Molecular and Cellular Biosciences Department at the University of Southern California.
The review is accepted, in the journal's Genetics of Aging section.
It is published, and Bioengineer.org covers it the same day.

mechanism.text: The review starts from the fact that mitochondria are inherited from the mother. In its words, this "limits selection on the mitochondrial genome to females, potentially leading to male-harming alleles". A variant that is harmless in daughters but hurts sons is invisible to selection, because sons never pass it on. That is the "mother's curse".

mechanism.h: Fisher's principle rewards the scarcer sex
mechanism.text: Fisher's principle says what happens when one sex becomes rare. The review puts it plainly: "A mutation that reduces the abundance of one sex increases the relative reproductive fitness of that sex, because that sex now has access to more mates. This leads to selection for parents that produce more of the limiting sex."

mechanism.h: A daughter-biased variant makes sons valuable
mechanism.text: In the review's first model, a mitochondrial variant, M2, makes mothers produce more daughters than sons. As M2 spreads, "males become relatively scarce and their reproductive fitness is increased." A nuclear gene that restores an even sex ratio then gains ground through Fisher's principle, which reins in M2's effect on sons.

mechanism.h: Killing too many males costs the mothers too
mechanism.text: The review's conclusion adds a direct brake. If a mitochondrial variant "eliminates or sterilizes the males, the reproductive fitness of the female is reduced because her eggs will not get fertilized." So selection in females cannot keep favouring a variant that removes too many males.

Put together, the review argues that "a balance between MC and FP could potentially produce stabilizing selection for moderately male-harming mitochondrial genome alleles". Its second and third models describe "direct selection" on M2 itself, under specific assumptions about which matings succeed.

predictions.text: No experiment will show a male-harming mitochondrial variant held at a stable intermediate frequency by sex-ratio selection, as the review's models propose. A peer-reviewed study showing it in any animal would prove this wrong.

limits: It is a review with models, not a new experiment. The central claim is stated as a hypothesis: "It is hypothesized that FP creates a limit to the male-harming effects of mitochondrial genome alleles resulting from MC."

The models rest on assumptions. In the first, an extra fitness cost for M2 "was found to be necessary to produce stabilizing selection", and the 20 percent used is called "illustrative". The second model's key incompatibility between M2 females and M2 males "has not been previously reported".

The data do not all fit. The review notes that some studies "have not observed the genetic variance in mitochondrial genome effects on male life span as might be expected for MC", and that some human studies have not found the variance in offspring sex ratio Fisher's principle would predict, possibly from "insufficient statistical power".
Fisher's principle is not the only brake on mother's curse. The review lists others, including rare transmission of mitochondria from fathers and nuclear "restorer" genes that act in males.

faqs.a: The idea that, because mitochondria are inherited only from mothers, variants in mitochondrial DNA that harm males but not females can spread. It is also called the Frank and Hurst hypothesis.

faqs.q: What does this have to do with aging?
faqs.a: The review starts from the idea that aging comes from genes whose effects conflict between life stages and between the sexes. It argues the balance between the two forces could also keep alive nuclear genes whose effects conflict between the sexes in ways that favour aging.

faqs.q: Did the study find this in people?
faqs.a: No. It reviews earlier studies in humans and model organisms and adds models. It says the human evidence on genes for offspring sex ratio still needs independent confirmation.

actions: If you read that Fisher's principle "restrains" harmful mutations, check whether the source is an experiment or a model. Here it is a model.
If you study mitochondrial variants in flies or other animals, the review's models say which sex-ratio data would test the idea.
When one sex becomes scarce in a population, ask what that does to each member's reproductive fitness. That is the lever Fisher's principle pulls.
whyItMatters: Fisher's principle is usually taught as the reason most species have about as many males as females. This review uses it as a working force: a pressure that pushes back on any gene that shifts the balance, including genes in the mitochondria that only mothers pass on.
